opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the basic dynamic is pretty simple. Generating code is becoming almost free. A coding agent can write thousands of lines in minutes, and that's only going to accelerate. But generating code was never really the bottleneck in software. The bottleneck is knowing whether the code is correct, whether it does what you actually wanted, and whether it breaks something else. When the cost of producing code drops by orders of magnitude, the relative cost of checking it goes way up. Verification becomes the scarce resource.

Today most verification is informal. You have a human reviewer reading a pull request, some unit tests, maybe some integration tests, and a lot of trust in the engineer who wrote it. That works when humans write code at human speed. It doesn't scale when an agent is producing a hundred PRs a day. Nobody can carefully review all of that, and if you just rubber-stamp it, you'll get subtle bugs and security issues piling up.

So you need much stronger, more automated ways of getting confidence. That ranges from better test generation, fuzzing, and static analysis all the way to formal methods: writing specifications and actually proving that an implementation satisfies them. Historically formal verification has been a niche, used for things like aerospace, chip design, cryptographic libraries, because it was extremely expensive. You needed experts spending months writing proofs for relatively small amounts of code. But the same models that write code are getting quite good at writing proofs too, in systems like Lean. So the cost of formal verification is coming down at the same time as the need for it is going up. That combination is what makes me think it becomes a much bigger industry.

There's also a nice feedback loop. Verification isn't just a safety net for agents, it's a training signal. If you have a checker that can tell you with certainty whether something is correct, you can do reinforcement learning against it. That's a big part of why models have improved so fast on math and code: those are domains where you can verify the answer. The more of software we can make verifiable, the better the agents get, and the more code they produce, which again increases demand for verification.

And I think the human role shifts accordingly. Instead of writing implementations, people will spend more of their time on specifications: saying precisely what the system should do, what invariants must hold, what's not allowed to happen. Then the agent writes the code and the proof, and a machine checks it. That's a very different way of building software, and there's a lot of tooling, infrastructure, and companies that need to exist to make it practical.

r001.rationale: The response says formal verification was historically niche because it was extremely expensive, requiring experts to spend months proving relatively small amounts of code.

fable-5.1.text:
So the simple way I think about it is: for a long time, the bottleneck in software was writing the code. That's what engineers spent most of their time on, and that's what most of the tooling was built around. Now, with coding agents, the cost of producing code is collapsing. You can generate a thousand lines in a few minutes, you can have an agent refactor an entire module overnight. And when the cost of producing something goes close to zero, the bottleneck moves to the next thing in the chain, which is: is this actually correct?

And that question becomes much harder, not easier, in this regime. When a human writes the code, there's an implicit review happening the whole time. The person understands why each line is there, they have a mental model of the system, they notice when something looks off. When an agent writes the code, that mental model doesn't exist anywhere on the human side. You get a huge diff, it compiles, the tests pass, and you have to decide whether to merge it. Reading it carefully would take almost as long as writing it yourself, so in practice people skim, or they trust the tests. That's a very fragile situation, especially as the volume goes up.

So I think the industry has to respond by making verification a first-class product, not an afterthought. And I mean this in a fairly broad sense. There's the formal end: proof assistants, model checking, things like Lean or specification languages, where you can actually get a guarantee. That used to be a niche academic activity because writing the proofs was extremely expensive. But models are getting quite good at this now. If an agent can write the code and also write a machine-checked proof that it satisfies the spec, that changes the economics completely. Then there's the less formal end: fuzzing, property-based testing, static analysis, agents whose only job is to adversarially attack the code that other agents produced. I think we'll see a lot of that, basically a generator-verifier split where you spend as much or more compute on checking as on generating.

And there's also a shift in what humans actually do. If you're not reading every line anymore, what you're writing is the specification, the invariants, the properties that must hold. So the skill moves from "how do I implement this" to "how do I state precisely what correct means." Which is harder than it sounds. Most of the bugs that matter are really specification bugs, where the code does what you said and not what you meant.

So when I say it becomes a much larger industry, I mean all of that: the formal tooling, the automated adversarial testing, the infrastructure to run it at scale, and the people who know how to write specs. Today that's a small corner of the field. I think in five years it's a huge part of what shipping software actually costs, because generation will be nearly free and trust won't be.

r001.rationale: The candidate says formal verification was niche because writing machine-checked proofs was extremely expensive, identifying the difficulty and cost of formal verification as a reason for its limited adoption.

astra-6.text:
I think the bottleneck is going to shift from writing code to knowing whether the code is correct. Today, the amount of software you can produce is constrained by the number of engineers you have. With coding agents, you can generate much more code, but you don’t automatically get a corresponding increase in your ability to check it.

And checking that something looks reasonable is very different from checking that it actually satisfies the requirements. You can run tests, but the tests only cover the cases you thought about. If an agent writes both the implementation and the tests, it can make the same incorrect assumption in both.

So I expect much more value to move toward verification: better testing, better specifications, and, where it makes sense, formal proofs. Those things can be expensive today, but the economics change when code generation becomes very cheap and you’re producing much more software. You still need a reason to trust what you deploy.

r001.rationale: The response says testing, specifications, and formal proofs can be expensive today, implying a cost barrier. It does not clearly identify the difficulty of formal verification as a major reason software verification has limited adoption.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the bottleneck is going to shift from writing code to knowing whether the code is correct. If you can have agents producing a lot of software very cheaply, you still need to establish that it does what you intended, that it’s secure, and that a change hasn’t broken something elsewhere.

And verification is often easier than generation. You might not know how to implement something yourself, but you can specify properties it should satisfy or check the result. So you can imagine agents writing code and other systems testing it, finding counterexamples, or proving certain properties about it.

The interesting thing is that even if verification becomes much cheaper per line of code, the total amount of code being produced could grow enormously. So I expect a lot more effort—and a much larger industry—around checking software.

r001.rationale: The response says verifying correctness is necessary as code production grows, but it does not identify the difficulty of formal verification as a reason software verification has had limited adoption.
